newsitem.title: VATICAN: Castro dazzles Italy, much moved by Pope.
newsitem.headline: Castro dazzles Italy, much moved by Pope.

text.p: Communist President Fidel Castro crowned a visit to Italy with a "miracle" meeting with Pope John Paul and promised him a royal welcome in Cuba.

The veteran revolutionary and the anti-communist crusader met for an historic first audience at the Vatican on Tuesday at which Castro issued an "unconditional" invitation to visit his Caribbean island. The Pope accepted and plans to go next year.
"For me it is a miracle that I have been able to greet the Pope," he added in remarks shown on Cuban state television.
Castro told a news conference in Rome after his 35-minute private audience that he had never dreamed of meeting the Pontiff, and saluted him as a figure of major world influence.
"I took the opportunity to reiterate my invitation to Cuba," Castro said. "He will be received like a king and with respect."

The Vatican visit, a major step forward in sometimes testy relations between the communist state and the Roman Catholic Church, capped a high-profile trip to Italy where Castro has been greeted like a superstar and clearly enjoyed the attention.
The 70-year-old president has been whisked around town in a huge motorcade complete with machine gun-toting police in tow.

He used his speech at a U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit in Rome last week to launch a stinging assault on the evils of capitalism, describing the gathering's aims as "shamefully modest" and hunger as daily genocide.
He also lashed out at Washington's 34-year trade embargo but sidestepped criticism over alleged human rights abuses and calls to implement more democratic reforms.
The U.S. State Department denied that the Pope's trip to Cuba would be a setback for its policy of isolating Castro.
"The Pope undoubtedly can play a constructive role in promoting democratic change and protecting human rights in Cuba," said spokesman Glyn Davies.

Anti-Castro Cuban exiles in the United States also gave a cautious welcome. "A visit by a pope with the record of this one in his fight against communism and dictatorship will certainly be positive," said Francisco Hernandez of the Cuban American National Foundation.

Castro thanked the Pontiff for the Vatican's firm opposition to the U.S. blockade and said there were no strings attached to next year's planned trip. Cuba is the only Spanish-speaking country in Latin America which the Pope has not visited.
"I did not put any conditions on the Pope and the Pope did not put any conditions on me either," Castro said.
Chief Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said both sides had agreed there would be no limitations on what the Pope could say or where he could go. No date has yet been fixed.

Castro, a revolutionary icon who flew to Rome in his trademark khaki military fatigues before swapping them for a sober business suit, caused a sensation in Italy, which once boasted the mightiest Marxist party in the West.

Tourists craned to get a glimpse of him, officials at the summit queued for autographs and one journalist was even rewarded with a kiss on the cheek at Tuesday's news conference after she asked him to pose for a souvenir photograph.

But Castro was equally bowled over by the magnificence of the Papal appartments and the splendour of St Peter's Basilica and the Sistine Chapel. "Una maravilla (a marvel)," he said to himself as he gazed at Michelangelo's Last Judgement fresco.
Some tourists were less impressed, however, when their own visit to St Peter's was interrupted by Castro's impromptu tour.
"Well I'll be damned!" said Emilia, an American from Florida on holiday with her husband Chester, after finding herself in Christendom's biggest church with the communist leader.
"He's an atheist. It's a wonder the church doesn't fall down."
